articleContract.title: AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says

story.title: AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says

facts.text: "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report.
"The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech."
Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back.

Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us.
Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.

AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).

Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.
Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group.
What: A Daily Spark note arguing that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to US companies outside tech.

Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed.
The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015.
These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.
Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.
The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology.
The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side.
Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending.
Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency.
The charts show correlation in time, not cause.

Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI.
The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits.
The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data.
The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist.
Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins?
A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are.
This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it.
For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.
Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 .

Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note.
When: Published October 24, 2026, following related Apollo notes on June 30 and August 9, 2026.
Where: The United States, with the analysis centred on S&P 500 companies and Ramp's business spending data.
